utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And if you would like to introduce yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My name is Marinko Palavra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Scott, was there something you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel Palavra, you have come here as a Court witness at the request of the Court, and the procedure we're going to follow is this: that the Court has read your testimony in the Blaskic trial, and that is part of the Court record, so there's no need to go over anything that you said there. But what we're going to do is to give the parties, that's the Prosecution and the Defence, the opportunity to ask you questions. When that is done, if there's anything you want to add, of course you'll have the opportunity to do so. So the procedure is that you'll be cross-examined first of all by the Prosecution and then by the Defence counsel for the two accused. Mr. Scott, it's for you to begin. How long do you anticipate being?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me. Your Honour, I think my examination of this witness will probably take most of the day, a good part of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could speed up as much as possible. We've got other things to deal with this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I can tell the Court that I've edited down and edited down, and I'll try to do that and I'll try to proceed as quickly as can be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, take the example of the other witness who took too long, in the opinion of the Chamber; that is, his cross-examination did. I think that for this witness we should go directly to what is crucial without elaborating on what we have already heard within this case. I think that in this way you will certainly be able to shorten your cross-examination so as to focus on what is essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Scott, you could briefly deal with the positions which the witness held during the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's where I was going to start, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Palavra.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As you heard this morning, we will try to move rather quickly through the opening parts of my questions. I hope we can do that and I hope you will find that perhaps they are not questions that will require a great deal of comment or any particular controversy, I hope, so we'll try to move quickly. And by the way, I should ask you, sir: What is your current rank? You are in the army or the military forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, my rank was frozen from the moment I joined the defence ministry of the Federation Army. Therefore, my rank is colonel, and it has been frozen until further notice. In the defence ministry of the Army of the Federation, there will be certain positions that will entail a military rank, but for the moment the situation is such that no one is given ranks in the defence ministry, but simply the positions they hold.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I was asking primarily at the moment so that I could address you appropriately, so I'll refer to you as colonel. Colonel, you are a Bosnian Croat, you were born in Travnik in 1959; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were jumping ahead to the rank and the position that will consume most of our examination today. I believe during 1993 and thereafter you served as the head of the 4th Battalion of Military Police of the HVO in Central Bosnia; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: It is, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at that time your rank, is it correct, was Major?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, when you testified in the Blaskic case, Colonel, in January of 1999, you described yourself at that time, if I understand correctly, as the overall chief of military police in the security sector of the HVO component of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct, and is that still correct today?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question. I didn't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand your current situation, sir. You described yourself previously as being the overall chief or the head, senior officer, of the military police and something called the security sector of the HVO component of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I understand now. You mean just now in the defence ministry of the Army of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No. I'm in the security sector, security and intelligence affairs sector, and within that there is a sector for the military police. So I'm in the department for security and intelligence affairs as head of the sector of military police, so the military police is within the department of security and intelligence affairs attached to the Defence Ministry. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And I also have my superior, my chief of the Security Service, and by his position he is assistant minister for security and intelligence affairs. There is an assistant and a deputy assistant. Just now, a Bosniak holds the position of assistant minister for intelligence affairs, that is, security affairs, and his deputy is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Part of what I'm trying to understand, if I can ask the question this way, you consider yourself at the moment and for the last several years, if I can put it this way, sir, are you in the military police business, or are you in the intelligence business, or both?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I am in the military police business.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, going back to your position with the 4th Battalion Military Police, you were the head of that military police unit for Central Bosnia from approximately the 1st of August, 1993, to the 27th of August, 1997, when you then moved to the Ministry of Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the time that you served in that position, the Central Bosnia operative zone included Vitez, Busovaca, Travnik, and Novi Travnik, Kiseljak, and Zepce; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, and Usora.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your position as the head of military police in that region, it covered all of those municipalities, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, backing up just for a few moments so we can put your involvement in the war in some broader context, if I understand it, sir, in April 1992, you were ordered by the HVO Travnik municipal command to form a police unit in Travnik, and you did that, and you became the commander of this police unit from April 1992 to September 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, from April?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have it, sir, that you were the -- you formed and then were the commander of this police unit in Travnik from approximately April 1992 to September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, that's not so. I formed the military police of the HVO, of the Municipal Staff of the HVO because before that I was in a school in Han Bijela. I was the school principal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand, sir. You formed this police unit, then, and how long were you in that position?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Throughout the period from 1992 in April until September 1992, I was in the military police. But in the beginning I formed the military police of the municipal HVO staff in agreement with the late commander, Ivica Stojak, and in the meantime, a Croat from the former Yugoslavia came, that is, from the former army, who had fled over to our side. His name was Bernard Martic. And I insisted that he should be the commander of the military police, and I his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Who gave you the order or direction to form the military police in Travnik, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I said it was given to me by the commander of the municipal HVO staff at the time, the late Ivica Stojak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then in about September of 1992, if I understand it, sir, is it correct that you transferred from this police force or unit to become the commander of the Special Purposes Unit, also attached to the Travnik municipal -- or excuse me, the Travnik police administration?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: In those days, Your Honours, a police administration was being formed in Travnik, the civilian police, and I was given the assignment to form a unit for special purposes attached to the Travnik police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The chief of the Travnik police administration was Mr. Ivo Rezo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What I'd like to ask you next, sir, this Travnik police administration, just so the Court and Judges are clear and the record is clear, you're not talking now about simply the municipality of Travnik, but as I understand, you can correct me if I'm wrong, the Travnik police administration was a regional police administration body, you might say, for Central Bosnia. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The Travnik police administration covered all the police stations in the area of Central Bosnia, that is, Busovaca, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Bugojno, Jajce, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that respect then, sir, you as the head or the commander of this special police unit that was formed were the head of a Special Police Unit that, again, ranged over Central Bosnia; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Our headquarters were in Travnik, and we were in Travnik. It is a special purpose unit. That is what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Before I continue on about that unit, was there a similar regional -- excuse me, a regional level agency or arm of the government called the Travnik defence administration? Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The defence administration for Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember. There may have been one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me associate it with a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll try to move on, Your Honour. These are ties in to questions that will come.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall there being a regional defence administration body that was headed, for interest, if it perhaps refreshes your memory, by Ante Puljic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the role of this special police unit that you commanded in Central Bosnia was? How was it different than the regular police? How was it different, if it was, from the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I was given the task to set up a special purposes unit attached to the police administration of Travnik. At first we were housed in the School of Music in Travnik and later we moved to the former Yugoslav People's Army centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to try not to interrupt you, but you've already heard the Judges say they want to move forward with some dispatch, and my question was not where the office of this police unit was housed. How was the functions -- how was what you did as commander of this special police unit for all of Central Bosnia, how was it different from the regular police; how was it different, if it was, from the military police? That's my question. If you could please confine your answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, the special purposes unit attached to the Travnik police administration determined the tasks according to orders given by Ivo Rezo, the chief of the department, and one of those tasks was escort and security of certain individuals, and all other assignments given by the chief of the police administration to me. This included going to the front lines, going to Jajce, to the defence lines, towards the Serbs, everything that the chief of the administration ordered us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving on, cutting across a number of questions here, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What you're telling us, then, is that -- is it correct, do I understand you correctly that through this period, then, from about September of 1992, approximately, when this special unit was formed, until the summer of 1993, you considered your superior to be and took direction and orders from and reported to Ivo Rezo; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is Mr. Rezo considered to be a civilian or a military person?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know how he was considered, but he was a civilian person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that Mr. Rezo had a close relationship or working relationship with Mr. Kordic, Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I know that while I was in the police administration in Travnik that the chief of the police administration, Ivo Rezo, would go frequently to see Mr. Kordic. But I was not present at any of their meetings. This was what I heard from Ivo Rezo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So according to Mr. Rezo himself, he told you that he was in frequent communication with and met frequently with Mr. Kordic. That's correct, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in early June of 1993, in connection with the action, military fighting around Travnik, the remainder, if you will, the surviving elements of the Travnik Brigade and also your special police unit withdrew or retreated from Travnik, we can say that, and you went to the Kraljevica area for a time, where you operated then under the commander, in some sense attached to what remained of the Travnik Brigade, until approximately 1 August 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Briefly -- please, briefly, Colonel, but was your unit not -- did you not retreat, you and your unit, from Travnik in about June of 1993? And please correct me where I've misstated.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I went to Kraljevica for the first time -- I think it was the month of May. I don't know. And I was there together with the special unit. Our task was to hold the defence line at Kalibunar up there, because the conflicts had already started between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm going to stop you there for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For these purposes, Your Honour, in light of the transcript, and again taking the Court's guidance to heart, I'm going to simply suggest --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Colonel, when you testified in the Blaskic case -- I'm referring to the LiveNote reference pages at 16682, 16763 -- you testified that in early June, when the Croats, HVO armed forces were retreating from Travnik, you withdrew with the remainder of your special police unit, you then operated as part of the residual, and I believe the residual was -- at least, the English translation of your word, the residual Travnik Brigade, and that you did that until approximately the 1st of August, 1993. Now, I put it to you, sir, that's your testimony from the Blaskic case. I think we can move -- let's just -- unless that's violently different than what you believe it to be, can we move on? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so I can follow along with this, could we have reference to the official transcript in Blaskic? I don't have the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Those are the only page numbers that I have, Your Honour. I have a transcript here, and the pages that I'm using are the ones that are on this transcript. I can't even tell you at the moment, but those are the page numbers I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, it's not a satisfactory situation when we don't have the same documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's the only transcript that I've ever been aware of, Your Honour, but we can check during a break. I can't very well deal with it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps counsel can tell me if his page 6 -- what he has on page 1673 [sic] talks about the -- or better, 16682 talks about the withdrawal of this unit from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the transcript which I have for this witness's evidence begins at 16678 and continues through until 16852.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's exactly what I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, what have you got?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think we have the same thing, Your Honour. I think the page numbers that you recited are precisely the ones that I have. I just don't see a reference on the pages that Mr. Scott cited to the testimony that the witness was giving. Maybe I missed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's not a matter which need detain us now. Let us move on. If need be, we can come back to it or you can come back to it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just turned to it. It's about the middle of page 16682. But as you say, we won't belabour it. My reference to LiveNote could have been a misnomer, Your Honour. If it was, I apologise for that. It appears that at least the Prosecution and the Chamber have the same transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's move on, Colonel. During this time period, and I'm now talking about the time between June of 1993 and August 1993, when you took up your position as head of chief of military police in Central Bosnia, or at least, excuse me, the 4th Battalion of Military Police, who were you, what were you doing in that interim period in terms of where was your unit engaged and who did you consider your superior to be at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: If you're thinking about the period from June to August, did you say, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Then up until June I was in Travnik, and my superior was the chief of the police department in Travnik, Ivo Rezo. When the Croats were expelled from Travnik, and of course my own units, part of the units went across Serbian territory, that is to say Vlasic, and I decided to go to the free territory under the control of the HVO. That means that part of the Travnik municipality -- that was part of the Travnik municipality with headquarters at Prahulje, and it is there that I met up with the commander of the Travnik Brigade, the late Jozo Leuter. Because Rezo, the chief of the police administration of Travnik, had probably made an agreement with the late Jozo that the units, the special purpose units, should be placed at the disposal of the Travnik Brigade or regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Colonel, and exactly that. Your Special Police Unit during that time period, then, was subordinated to and for all practical purposes became part of an HVO military brigade, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: A part of the units, the unit which passed into free territory under the control of the HVO, and following the daily Muslim attacks at that time, I placed myself at the disposal of the commander of the Travnik Brigade, and I took up my position at the defence line straight away with my own unit and made up a defence against the further Muslim attacks on the areas -- defending the areas which were still under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Colonel. So the answer to my question is "yes." During this time period, did you ever attach yourself or take orders or direction from the Vitez Brigade and Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you withdrew or when the special forces withdrew from Travnik, you have testified in the Blaskic case that you received an order from Ivo Rezo about this withdrawal, and you further said that the withdrawal from Travnik, at least in that respect, was a decision that had been made by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm referring to, for the Chamber and counsel, page 16.766.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you understood that a civilian government decision had been made to retreat or withdraw from Travnik, who did you -- what civilian authorities, what political authorities did you understand to be involved in making that decision?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I truly don't understand the questions. They're not clear enough, but I'll tell you what I do know. I was -- stayed on last in Travnik with the Special Police. It was referred to the special unit for special purposes, the Special Purposes Unit in fact. Everybody had left Travnik and moved towards Kalibunar, and the Travnik Brigade was displaced as well. Only the police administration, that is to say, this special unit of which I was in command, we were the only ones to stay on in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Who told you to stay on in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Nobody told me, I just stayed on myself, and we went on with our work. Two days later, I was told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't bother about that. If there's any other questions arising, they can be asked. Colonel, if you would just keep your answers as short as you can and to the point, we'll get on quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Colonel, let me suggest that we've covered the point about your withdrawal and the fact that you then became attached to this other -- what was left of the Travnik Brigade under Mr. Leutar. You've said that. My question to you now, and you testified in the Blaskic case, I'm referring again to 16.766, that the decision -- or your answer was, let me just do it this way: "I really don't know, but I think that after the civilians left Travnik and the army left Travnik towards the Serb-held territories at that time, this was decided upon of the government of the HVO, and this was under the control of the civilian authorities." My question to you, my exact question to you is, who were the civilian authorities, who or what? What persons made this decision to withdraw from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know or hear that Mr. Kordic was involved as one of the decision-makers, that the HVO forces should withdraw?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm just probing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You did not ever hear, it was never part of, in your subsequent experience as chief of military police or anything else in your military experience in Central Bosnia, you did not come to know that Mr. Kordic was involved in that decision. That's my only remaining question. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. My last question, then, on this topic before moving on is, when the Croats -- when at least part of, and I realise there were different groups, but you testified earlier that approximately 25.000 of the Croats who withdrew from Travnik, withdrew from Travnik through Serb lines or Serb-controlled areas. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but they were not withdrawing. They had been expelled and were fleeing from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. I'll use your word in this instance. They fled through into Serb-controlled areas and across Serb lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I said that. I was clear then and I'm clear now. A part of them went across the area controlled by the Serbs, Serb-held territory, and a part of the Croats and those units went the other way towards the Lasva Valley. I decided to go towards the Croats, and that's how I arrived in Nova Bila at Prahulje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, moving on. Then going to April -- excuse me, August of 1993, you were named by then Colonel Blaskic to be the chief of the 4th Battalion Military Police; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I received a temporary order from Colonel Blaskic as the chief of the Military Police battalion, 4th Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can move quickly at this point, Colonel, if possible, just by way of background, would it be correct that the 4th Battalion Military Police had been established in Central Bosnia, that is, the Central Bosnia operative zone of the HVO, in approximately September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's move on. Is it correct, then, do you have a recollection today, can you help us with this, that from the time of its establishment, the commanders of the 4th Battalion Military Police in approximately this order were Ivan Lalic followed by Zvonko Vukovic, who also testified in this case. Mr. Vukovic continued in that position until approximately mid-January of 1993, and at that time Mr. Vukovic was replaced by Pasko Ljubicic. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then it was Mr. Ljubicic that you replaced as the head of that battalion in approximately the 1st of August, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, sir, on the 1st of August, 1993, you've testified previously Blaskic came to you, you said that you were being given the most responsible task to perform in the operative zone. The gist of it was there had been, and you knew there to be -- to have been, a number of problems in the HVO, particularly in the military police and some of the special units, and Colonel Blaskic essentially came to you, wanted you to take over and, if I could use the terms, clean up or correct the problems in the HVO -- in much of the HVO in Central Bosnia. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is not correct. Blaskic did not come to me, but I went to Blaskic. And before that, what happened before that, once the Croats had been expelled from Travnik, I have already said that I placed myself at the disposal of the commander of the Travnik Brigade with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the remainder of the units, and in actual fact, we took up our positions at the defence line straight away facing the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour this is not responsive --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do not want the Prosecution penalised by the non-responsive --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Just a little patience, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, both of you. Don't interrupt, first of all. Let the witness finish and continue in the way he has been. But Colonel Palavra, would you bear in mind that we do need to get on, so concentrate on answering the questions. Now, continue your reply.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Briefly, this is how it was: Colonel Blaskic did not come to the Travnik Brigade, but someone from the Security Service came. His name was Anto Sliskovic, and the operational officer, I think it was Pilicic at the time, so they came to the Travnik Brigade, the two of them, because at a meeting in the operative zone for Central Bosnia, that is to say, all the brigade commanders, together with Colonel Blaskic, of 10 or 11 candidates who for the post of commander of the military police, allegedly they had selected me. On the basis of that decision and for that reason, they came to the Travnik Brigade, that is to say, these two officers came, and Colonel Blaskic agreed with me as their choice. So they came to ask me whether I agreed to take up that duty. And when I said that I agreed, after a certain amount of time, I had a meeting in Vitez with Colonel Blaskic, and it was there that we started a working meeting. We had a working meeting, and his vision and my own vision of what a future military police should look like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And he told you, sir, and I'm referring to page 16.685, he told you that he was -- that you had the most responsible task to perform, the most responsible function in the operative zone, to carry out, as you said it, to create this new vision or implement this new vision that the two of you apparently share for the military police in Central Bosnia; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, it is. In the talk he told me, in our conversation he told me, that I had one of the most responsible tasks to perform at that particular moment, for that moment in the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Colonel, he told you at that time, and we're going to come back to this later, but I simply want to mention it before moving on now, that he told you or you knew at that time -- let me rephrase that. You knew at that time that Colonel Blaskic was not happy with Pasko Ljubicic, didn't you; and you so testified in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Well, probably he was not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. To the extent we need to, we'll come back to that. Now, you were named to this post, first, as you say, temporarily, but you remained in the post until August of 1997, so it wasn't too temporary. But you were named to this position by -- essentially by Colonel Blaskic, and the reason so is because essentially at that time, the Central Bosnia operative zone was cut off in many respects from Mostar and from other authorities, and the first -- or HVO government or military authorities, and you've indicated that it was primarily for this reason essentially that it was Blaskic who appointed you and Blaskic to whom you were subordinate. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Blaskic gave me this temporary appointment as chief of the 4th Military Police Battalion, and this was confirmed from the military police administration later on by the head of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps it would be helpful if we would turn to some of the documents, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown, there is -- a binder of some documents, Your Honours, have been prepared to facilitate the review. These are some basic military police documents. They were assembled to make it hopefully easier as reference tools, and if one of those could be provided to the witness, and particular attention to Exhibit 1134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are documents which have already been produced, are they, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Many of them have been, Your Honour. Some of them are new.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise. Many of them the Court will have seen before; some of them are new, Your Honour. This one I believe the Court will have seen before, 1134. I would direct the Court's attention and the counsel's attention to page 8 of the English translation, the first paragraph starting on that page. Unfortunately, obviously, I'm not able to -- I apologise, but I'm not able to direct Colonel Palavra in the B/C/S version to that exact same reference. Perhaps the translation can help me if I simply do it -- we have the English version on the ELMO. I'm now looking at page 8 of 1134. It doesn't look like my page. That's not the page 8. You can hand the usher the whole thing, please. If the usher can assist, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This indicates, Colonel, is -- and I'll just read it, perhaps is the easiest thing to do, and the translation, the interpreters can assist you. It says, "Owing to the isolation of the Central Bosnia operative zone, contact between the military police administration and the 4th Battalion was possible only by technical means of communication and radio communications. All the powers of the chief of military police administration in this operative zone were transferred to the assistant chief for Central Bosnia operative zone, Mr. Pasko Ljubicic." Do you see that, sir? And that is correct, isn't it? Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say something in this regard? I don't understand English, but Pasko Ljubicic, the moment that I arrived as commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion, he received -- he was given a new role. Because of the impossibility of communication and because the military police administration was cut off and with the -- and communication with the battalions, the 4th Military Police Battalion, and Pasko was appointed the assistant chief for Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And I think on that point, Colonel, at the end of the day we are in agreement. And it was because of this fact that Central Bosnia, as you've just stated, was cut off in this respect, that you testified in the Blaskic case at page 16.683, that it was largely because of that that you were appointed, at least initially, by Blaskic to take charge of the head of military police. Isn't that correct, sir? It may have been confirmed by other authorities later, but initially it was by Colonel Blaskic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I was clear. At the meeting in the operative zone, at least that is what I was told, the brigade commanders who were in action in the operative zone of Central Bosnia, they proposed me to be the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion. There were about 11 candidates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to go over that, Colonel. We've already dealt with it. I think, Mr. Scott, we've gone on enough about that. We can see what the reply was in Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's essentially consistent with what the witness is saying now, whether it's called a temporary appointment or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And my -- we seem to have gotten hung up on this -- what was temporary and not temporary. The point of it was, and I do agree that perhaps it's been established, is that because, as the witness has testified, of the isolation of Central Bosnia, that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You then went on to say -- if I can move on then, from that point, Your Honours -- that same situation continued to be true with you, didn't it, Colonel? You found yourself in a situation where you did not have any regular communication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: May I take care of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, please. I'm sorry. I thought Judge Bennouna had a question. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was also the case, was it not, sir, that the same situation that we've been talking about for the last few moments applied to you, and in fact, you testified in the Blaskic case that you had no communications with the head office of the military police, and this continued until early 1994. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes. In essence, that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you testified that "Since there was no physical link with the military police administration in Mostar, we remained detached in the territory of Central Bosnia." So the most responsible individual in the zone of responsibility was the commander of the Operative Zone to whom you were subordinated; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, about this time that you became the commander of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police, Vladimir Santic became the deputy commander of that battalion, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I came on the 1st of August, Vlado Santic had been appointed temporarily, and I think for some 15 days he was the acting temporary commander of the 4th Police Battalion. The moment I arrived in Vitez, I took over the duties of commander, and Vlado Santic stayed on as my deputy, so he was my assistant or, rather, deputy throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how long did that continue to be the case, sir? How long did Mr. Santic continue as your deputy?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Santic was my deputy until he filed a request to go to the civilian police. Before the war he used to be in the civilian police, and as soon as conditions were such that he could go back to his former duties in the civilian police -- I think he left in 1995 or something like that. I don't know the exact date. But until then he was my deputy throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like you to please be shown Exhibit 2340. It's also in the binder -- it should be the last exhibit in the notebook -- in the binder that's been given to Chamber and counsel. 2340.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While that's being done, something for the legal officer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is: This is a document titled "Instructions to Military Police on Implementation of Law, of Criminal Procedure in Case of War or Immediate Threat of War to Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Now, in the course of your duties as head of the military police in Central Bosnia, did you see -- come to be familiar with this document or have occasion to use this document, sir? The question pending is: Are you familiar with that document, having seen it in the course of your duties as chief of the military police in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were a number of instructions. Probably this was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come back to that later. Let me ask you this. I'm sorry. Allow me to follow up in this respect, then. It's correct, isn't it, sir, that, as you said, there were a number of instructions, but the military police were supposed to enforce military law and military discipline? And if we took the time, which we won't because of the limits of time, to look at this document, it would take us through many instances about the way in which military police functions would be carried out and the nature of those functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we would just look at -- I think it's worth stopping for a moment, Your Honour, if we look at the first page, not the cover or title page, but the first page. It talks about the protection of people and property, it talks about the -- item G: "Shall verify, discover, send or bring HVO members who have left their unit or institution without authorisation." Number H: They provide physical protection to command post and senior officials, et cetera, et cetera. The document goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But you certainly understood that in fact it was a primary function of the military police to enforce -- to investigate violations of and enforce military discipline; isn't that correct, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I'm afraid I don't understand at all what the Prosecutor is asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, it may be better if you took the matter simply. I don't suppose there's any dispute about that. They were there to investigate the violations and enforce military discipline. Have you got any point on the document you can take --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not at this moment, Your Honour, other than to have established that the witness is familiar with this document or documents like it for the moment. I would not have thought it would be a point of any great contest, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I also want you to look, sir, at Exhibit 2332 in that binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm skipping over a couple, Your Honour, because of time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to see -- and maybe it's worth identifying for the record, because there's only one original of this document, Your Honour. Exhibit 2332 is a document that's titled "Three Years of Military Police." The original B/C/S version, Your Honour, looks like this. There should be a copy of it in the record, a black-and-white copy in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Colonel Palavra, you're familiar with this document, aren't you, and in fact you contributed one of the articles in this document? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what I've done, Your Honours, in the Court, and in the event it comes up in the course of the witness's examination today or, for that matter, in the Defence examination, English translations of some of these articles have been -- follow in the notebook, and they've, for reference, been called -- the first one is 2332A, the second is 2332B, and so forth. And if I could direct both the witness and Chamber's attention, please, to 2333 -- excuse me -- 2332D, as in "dog." That is an English translation, Your Honours, of the article written by Mr. Palavra, which I mention now because various statements by Colonel Palavra in the course of that -- in that document may come up in the remainder of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, moving on, then, to the command and control of the military police. In carrying out the normal military duties, the military police was daily responsible in terms of their daily tasks in concrete terms to the Operative Zone; is that correct, sir? Sorry. It has nothing to do with the article now, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if the usher can remove it for the time being if it may avoid distraction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in carrying out the normal duties of the military police, you and the units of the military police in Central Bosnia were subordinate to the Operative Zone and to the command of the Operative Zone; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've testified in the Blaskic case that the HVO military police operated on a territorial principle: Wherever there were HVO units, there were military police units, and the military police units were subordinate to the commanders of the HVO units, including at the brigade level; the brigade military police were subordinate to the brigade commanders. Is that true, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, no. We had units in Ravno Brcko that didn't have any military police. There was a territorial organisation where it existed, that is, in the areas of Central Bosnia, which belonged to the 4th Military Police Battalion. That was the 1st Company, the 2nd Company and the 3rd Company of the Military Police. The 1st Military Police Company was located in the Lasva Valley; the 2nd Company in the area of Kiseljak and Kresevo and the rest of Fojnica, what remained of Fojnica, and Vares; and the 3rd Company covered the area of responsibility of Zepce, the free parts of Tesanj and Usora and Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to rephrase the question, then, sir. In the areas in which there were HVO brigades operational, such as in Vitez, for instance, the military police in the brigades were subordinate to the brigade commander; isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was true throughout 1993 and continued into 1994; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The brigade police was accountable to the brigade commanders in daily police operations, and it is common knowledge what the task of the military police was: to arrest people, take them into custody, to provide security for headquarters and commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, then. Your Honour, in light of that question, I'm going to, at least momentarily, jump over about five exhibits, if that's -- if I understand the witness's answer correctly. If the witness could be shown 1172.3, 1172.3, which should be in the first bundle of -- separate from the notebook. While that's being done, I simply note for the record, maybe the best way, in terms of time, to move would be -- Your Honour, in this bundle of documents, which I had intended to go through the witness -- perhaps it's not necessary -- but 581.2, 371.1, 527.2, and 553 are all documents which the Prosecution would argue, would submit, establish the proposition that the military police were subject to -- were subordinate to the brigade commanders. Each of those documents support that proposition. Exhibit -- I will tell for the Cerkez counsel, Exhibit 553 is an order by Mr. Cerkez on the 18th of March, 1993, which the Chamber, I'm sure, has probably seen, will recall seeing before. Now, with that in mind, if I could ask the witness to look at Exhibit 1172.3, which should be the last exhibit in that bundle. 1172.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is an order by Colonel Blaskic, dated the 18th of August, 1993, to the commanders of the brigades in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and he says, "I hereby order," and item number 1, "the Brigade Military Police comes under the immediate command of the Brigade Commander," and so on. "as part of the established chain of the brigade and has the same status as other brigade units." Now, sir, that order by Colonel Blaskic on the 18th of August was confirming and in fact was what your experience had been throughout 1993, and that is that the military police were subordinate to the brigade commanders; is that correct? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes. The brigade police belonged to the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, at the time of the -- about the time that the military police was being reorganised in Central Bosnia, when you became the chief of that unit, there was also at that time formed, as part of the -- out of the military police or as part of the military police, something called the 3rd Light Assault Battalion. That's correct, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, there was a 3rd Light Assault Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I mention this only to avoid confusion, and I don't know if the Chamber has had this come up before. It probably has after all this time. But there was a time in which the 4th Battalion of the Military Police, the number reference changed to it being the 7th Battalion. That's correct, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're talking about the same unit. And in fact later, or some months later, in fact, the unit reference was changed back to 4th Battalion of the Military Police; isn't that correct? Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes. The 4th became the 7th and then it went back from the 7th to the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But about that time, as you've just indicated, something called the 3rd Light Assault Battalion was formed. And is it correct, sir, that that was formed and became under the command of Vlado Cosic from out of the military police in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: The 3rd Light Assault Unit was formed -- I do not recollect the exact date -- and the commander of that 3rd Light Assault Unit was Vlado Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I don't think it needs to be belaboured, Your Honours, but for the record, I would refer the Chamber and counsel to Exhibit 1165.2, which is also in the notebook, 1160 -- it's the third tab of the binder, Your Honour, and I think the Court will see that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise. It's hard always to be at the microphone and with the documents at the same time, but I apologise. The witness may simply refer to that if he wishes, but I would just tell the Chamber, represent to the Chamber, this is an order, then, by Valentin Coric, as the head of the military police administration in Mostar, which establishes -- dated the 12th of August, 1993, I should add -- which establishes and takes -- essentially puts into action the steps that we've talked about in the last few minutes, including the changes in Central Bosnia, as the Court can there see. And I think, Your Honours, again that may or may not come up in subsequent examination, but I think that's a good summary of this particular step of the organisation of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Changing subjects and getting started on a different topic before the -- presumably before the recess, Colonel: During the time that you were in Central Bosnia in 1993, were you familiar with and did you have occasion to interact with something called the Security and Information Service, or sometimes often abbreviated and called SIS?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the moment I took up duty as commander of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police, I established contact with the Security Service attached to the Operative Zone, and every morning at briefings with Colonel Blaskic -- his assistant for security was present at our early morning briefings, and at those briefings there was the assistant for security, there was me as the commander of the Military Police, and all the other assistants of Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And sir, the assistant for security that you've been talking about in the last few minutes, that was Anto Sliskovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that's so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the functions that the two of you performed, you and the military police, Mr. Sliskovic, and the Security and Information Service, the functions you performed often were related and often overlapped, in terms of ensuring, for instance, such things as security in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I had military police duties, and I worked on those exclusively, and that is the organisation worked on activities of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. My question was, though, was it not the fact, was it not the case, that in fulfilling those or carrying out those functions, you had frequent interaction with Mr. Sliskovic and the security and information service?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I said, Your Honours, I had the morning briefings where we were together, and sometimes after the briefings we would be in the office of the assistant for security. That depended on the situation and the assignments we were given and that cropped up at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, let's move forward. Mr. Sliskovic, did he have a deputy, his own deputy, just as you had Vlado Santic as your deputy, did Mr. Sliskovic during this time period have his deputy for SIS?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't believe so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's correct, is it not, sir, that there was an SIS officer at each level of the HVO organisation or structure, if you will? For instance, at the brigade level -- for instance, in the brigade, at each brigade, there was an SIS assistant or officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, apart from Mr. Sliskovic, did you come to have -- did you have any, you or your staff, your military police command staff, have any interaction with other representatives or officers of SIS, apart from Mr. Sliskovic in 1993? For instance, did you know someone named Miso Mijic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, I did know Miso Mijic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was his position, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Mr. Miso's position and function is something that is not clear to me even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He was an SIS officer, too, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know that. That is how he introduced himself. My task, Your Honours, was, as the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion, to cooperate and to work with the assistant for security affairs attached to the operative zone of Central Bosnia, and that meant with Anto Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Court wishes we could stop there. I apologise, I thought the witness was finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: What Miso claimed to be and what he actually did, I really don't know. I know that he did, and I know that he was under the protection of Kraljevic. As for his real functions, I really don't know what he did. I know that he was not part of the military organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn there for half an hour. Colonel Palavra, would you remember in this and any other break not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I'm sorry we've kept everybody waiting. We had to attend a Tribunal function.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I'm handing out now a second bundle of documents, a small bundle that -- for the next series of questions to counsel and the Chamber, and as far as I'm concerned, the entire bundle can be put in front of the witness at one time as well so it will make us move more quickly. While we're doing that, Your Honour, I've already skipped over before the break 1176.5, but the witness did agree that there were SIS officers in each brigade. This makes reference to apparently the death in August of Mr. Cerkez's security assistant or SIS officer. I think the Chamber may have seen that document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you say Mr. Cerkez's assistant. Yes, I see. This is Mr. Josic about whom we have had some evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And this is a letter from Mr. Sliskovic to the Vitez Brigade commander, Mario Cerkez, personally, "My condolences on the death of your security assistant."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Colonel, in terms of these -- the number of people associated with the security information service, I simply don't have time to argue with you about each of these, I'm simply going to ask you if you know these individuals or not in your capacity as chief or head of military police for Central Bosnia. Now, you knew Marijan Biskic, didn't you? He was a senior HV Croatian army officer who was involved with the military police on the Herceg-Bosna HVO Main Staff, and you knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did know Biskic. And when the conflict ceased between the Muslim forces, the BiH army, and the HVO, that's when I got to know him first in Posusje, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you knew, sir, that in 1993 in fact, he was an HV, that is, a Croatian army military police official who was serving on the HVO Main Staff. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not know that, but all I know is that Marijan Biskic originated from Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is to say, he is a Bosnian Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will simply refer the Court to Exhibit 2 -- Z2332, English translation H, out of this document for a statement about Mr. Biskic being with the military police of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you know who Ivo Lucic was -- Ivica Lucic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I did know, that is to say, I didn't know him personally, but I knew of him. I knew of Ivica Lucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He was the head of SIS in Mostar, in some respects you might say, at least on an organisational chart, Mr. Sliskovic's boss, isn't that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. true, Ivica Lucic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to interact with Mr. Lucic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I said I didn't know him personally. I just met him once. I was in Mostar, and I talked to him once. That is to say, we became acquainted, nothing more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you come to know an SIS official named Milenko Rajic? Representing -- Mr. Rajic was initially a senior SIS official and then became the chief in 1994 following Mr. Lucic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I met Rajic, too, during the celebration of the Security Service in Mostar. I think that was in 1996. But otherwise, I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know that he had become the chief of SIS following Mr. Lucic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I knew that through Anto Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We mentioned before the break Mr. Miso Mijic. I will ask the witness if you have the bundle in front of you, sir, if you could turn to Exhibit Z1354.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for the Chamber and counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document has not previously been provided to us, and therefore I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can't find it. Whereabouts is it, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's in the bundle that was handed out a few moments ago, Your Honour. It should be the second to last bundle. There's only about five documents there. It's a Zagreb document, Your Honour, and I believe it has been -- I believe it was disclosed some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I can't find it at the moment. Let me see if it's in the bundle. 1354, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: .1. Yes, I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might be heard briefly on this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I've been -- we're going to be filing our response for the Zagreb materials proposals this afternoon. I've been very intimately involved in reviewing the documents that have been provided to us, trying to figure out which order they've been provided in. We decided to make a chronological list, for the Court's convenience, of all of the documents that have been identified by the Prosecution, and this is not one of them. In addition, it does not have the stamp on the corner referred to by Mr. Nice yesterday as an archival stamp. This is not a Zagreb document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They're not all stamped --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with this in this way. We know there's been some evidence about Mr. Mijic. His name appears in relation to the evidence of Mr. Breljas. Now, beyond that, at the moment I'm not sure that we're going to be helped by the production of more documents on this particular topic. Mr. Scott, you can consider the objection for the moment. We won't admit it. If in due course you have some further information about it and it really is of importance, we'll consider it, probably when we consider the Zagreb documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And only five seconds, Your Honour. That's exactly the reason it's coming up for this witness, is because the Chamber will -- I forecast that the Chamber will see Mr. Mijic's name on a number of the Zagreb documents, and this witness is in a position to know and has said that he did in fact know Mr. Mijic, and that's the reason for these documents. But we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you also -- did you know an SIS operative in Central Bosnia named Boris Adzaip. And forgive me if I've pronounced it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the name is Boris Adzaip. Was that the name you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know at all where he worked or who he worked with, but I do know the man from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, again, we would tender -- we've given the Court and we point -- direct the Court to Exhibit 1230.3 and again 1354.1, which the chief of SIS, Mr. Lucic, who the witness has -- in fact, mentions both Mijic and Adzaip, and again my apologies, as being SIS operatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we also have an objection with respect to this document, due to the fact that in the translation it says in the upper right-hand corner that there is the handwritten signature of Marijan Cerkez [As interpreted]. If that is the translation, when I look at the original, there is no way in which a translator can determine whose signature it is, nor is he authorised to do so. So that should not be part of the translation, that remark in the upper right-hand corner. All I think that can stand there is illegibly handwritten. The person can't know whose the signature in fact is. And I make the objection because we have received many documents of a similar nature, where translators translate illegible signature and interpret it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a matter for evidence and not for interpretation. I agree. Now, Mr. Scott, we're going through this exercise, and I wonder where we're going and how we are being assisted by all this detail about the SIS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me be extremely transparent, Your Honour, about this. There are a number of the Zagreb documents and other documents coming from the archives that have these individuals' names on them. In the past several months the Defence has objected that they don't know who these people are, they don't know who wrote the document, they don't know whose initials are on the documents. I'm only taking this witness through a list of names of the SIS people who were active in Central Bosnia. This man, as the chief of military police, should know, or at least there's a basis to believe he should know who these people are, and simply putting the questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we not do it quite simply by saying, whatever your case is about these people, put it to the witness? The SIS consisted of X, Y, and Z, and then he can comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd be happy to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know, sir, during 1993, that in addition to the people we've named so far, that there was also a Bruno Saric, also a Dragan Voloder, also a Damir Smoljic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Damir Smoljic, who were again all SIS officers, operatives, agents, whichever term you might prefer, in Central Bosnia during 1993 and the first half of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I personally know Bruno Saric, but truly I did not know what he did in 1993. I know that they were protected by the late Kraljevic, the commander of the Vitezovi, and that they were with him, he was with them, but in my area of responsibility and the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia of the day, they were not in the military section there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in addition, we would point the Court again to the exhibits in the bundle, including also 1343.1, and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to Exhibit Z1343.1, Your Honour, that's yet another document that's never previously been provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The same ruling will apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you know Ivica Bandic? Was he an SIS operative in Central Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: What name did you say? Ivica -- what was the surname?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ivica Bandic.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You did not know, as head of military police, that Mr. Bandic was travelling, active in Central Bosnia during that time, allegedly investigating HVO war crimes, including Ahmici and Stupni Do? You were the head of military police, sir, and you weren't aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll come back to that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What position, if any, are you familiar with that a man named Tomislav Vlajic held in 1993, Tomo Vlajic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, could you assist us, assist the Chamber? You are in the process of asking the witness about a certain number of names, of details. Could you please present the issue to us first, tell us what it's about. As you said about the SIS, the information service, you put the questions within a certain context. So before going into detail, tell us what it is that you are trying to know with respect to this case and from this witness and then go to the details, and not the other way around, because otherwise it is difficult for us to follow. We are jumping from one detail to another without having the global picture of what you are trying to find out from this witness, and I think you will be helping us to focus on this in the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. I'm happy and anxious to assist the Chamber in any way that I can. What I had answered in response to Judge May's question is that these are individuals who the Prosecution will submit and will take the position over time and in our closing submissions, these were SIS officials who were active in Central Bosnia and who authored a number of reports during 1993 and 1994. And the Defence has already raised objections about some of these people and we're trying to identify them to assist the Court in identifying and providing some information. And it was our position and it was my assessment that this man, who was a senior HVO military officer, the head of all military police in Central Bosnia, would be in a position to know who these people are, and I believe he does know who they are. That's my position. And I put it to him, I put it to the witness that he is not being candid with us about that. Let me give the Court one example, Judge Bennouna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think there's a need to argue the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Scott. If the documents show that members of the SIS were acting in a particular capacity or that people were a member of the SIS, why do we need to go through the exercise of oral testimony on the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- maybe one document. It may assist the Court, maybe it doesn't. If it doesn't, I'll go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the document? Let's refer to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 1317.2. You don't have it right now, Your Honour. I'm trying to give the Court an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 1317.2. If I can have the usher's assistance. In the interests of speed, if I could just put this one on the ELMO. Because otherwise, Your Honour, we'll be fumbling with documents for some minutes. This is Exhibit, for the record, 1317.2. And if the usher could just please help me with putting this page on the ELMO, just this page. Your Honour, this -- what's been put on the ELMO is an exhibit. It's a report about Ahmici. You can see that from the top of the page. Down below that in the lower left corner are the initials "IB," and "A," "CH." And it's the Prosecution's position, Your Honour, that IB is Ivan or Ivica Bandic who was an SIS official in Central Bosnia. There's a number of documents bearing his initials and bearing his name, and that's what I'm putting -- I was trying to put to this witness. Now, the witness is telling me he doesn't know, but I thought I was entitled to at least ask the question, and that's why it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But it could be done without reference to the documents simply by asking the witness in each case, "Were these officials members of the SIS," and then you can read out the list one by one for his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel Palavra, you are going to hear a list of people. You will answer whether they were members of the SIS or not, or whether you don't know. Yes, Mr. Scott, if you'd like to put your list, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Some of them we've already touched on. Let me just back up to one, then. I'd ask you, sir, about Dragan Voloder and Damir Smoljic. Did you know either of those two individuals to be SIS officials active in Central Bosnia in 1993 or 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No. I personally know Dragan Voloder within the position of the Security Service attached to the operative zone, but none of them were operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was his position, then, if you knew Mr. Voloder personally?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me when I say I don't know. I said that certain people like Mijic, Voloder, and like the other one, Saric, they were protection for Kraljevic. They were with Kraljevic in his unit. That's where they were. I don't know where their seat was. I don't know where the seat of the SIS was either, if it existed, because you focussed on the Security Service attached to the operative zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I asked you earlier about Ivica Bandic, and I believe your answer was that you were not familiar with Mr. Bandic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: That's right. I don't know the man at all. Possibly I do, but I don't. I'd like to be able to identify him, but I just can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Palavra, in view of your position and your responsibilities, were you in contact with the SIS, the information service, and did you know the people working in that service?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did have contact with the Security Service within the operative zone of Central Bosnia. Therefore, for all my contacts, I went through Anto Sliskovic, the assistant for security affairs in the operative zone. He was the assistant of Colonel Blaskic at the time. So that was my level of contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but my question, Colonel Palavra, is, could you tell the Chamber which are the people that you knew and who were members of this SIS, this secret service or information service? Could you tell us, apart from Mr. Sliskovic, who are the persons that you knew who were members of this information service?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: In those days, that is, as of 1993 in the Security Service within the operative zone, I knew Anto Sliskovic, he was the assistant for security. I knew Tomo Vlajic. I knew Skocibusic, and they had a secretary, a lady.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And outside the operative zone, the central SIS, did you know people from that service beyond the local level, beyond the operational zone level?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Truly, I didn't have any contact with them. They had an assistant for security. Every brigade had an assistant security --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking you, Colonel, whether you had contact with them. I'm asking you whether you knew them. Could you tell us from your recollection the people that you knew from the information service at the central level, even if you were not in contact with them.
