I know that at the time that Zuti and Darko Kraljevic did act on their own initiative, and I assume to calm things down and in view of the general blockade by the Croats -- of the Croats by Muslim units, Colonel Blaskic appointed Zuti probably to calm him down or to win him over to his side. But I can tell you with full responsibility, it says here that the appointment is to the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. Zuti never spent a single day in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, nor did he have his office in the headquarters of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That's enough on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My last question is -- my last document is Exhibit 1075.1, which has also been previously admitted. It should be in the same bundle if they were -- I'm sorry. Here it is. 1075.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it not the case, sir, that this Darko Kraljevic, on the 18th of June, 1993, or around this same time, was promoted as deputy chief of the Central Bosnia SIS?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I just object to the form of that question, Your Honour. It actually says "deputy chief of the SIS centre," and I think that the witness testimony establishes that "SIS" and the "SIS centre," as envisaged by Judge Bennouna's questions, are two completely different entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The document is in front of everyone, Your Honour, simply. It didn't suggest otherwise, nor I'm not sure that the witness did say they were two separate things. I'm not sure he ever answered that question this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the Central Bosnia SIS centre, to follow up on counsel's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Come on. Let's get on with this. Do you know anything about this at all? If you don't, just say "no."

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know anything about this. This is for me null and void, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: It's quite insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I wonder if you could just move the ELMO so I can see the colonel. Thank you. Mr. President, I'd just like to pass out a bundle of exhibits that I have, eight separate documents that I may refer to during the course of this witness's testimony, and we also have copies for the translators if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, the one question that you weren't asked by the Prosecution today was this: Did you ever, as commander of the 4th Battalion of Military Police, later the 7th Battalion and then which reverted to the 4th Battalion again, did you ever take any orders, directions, or instructions from Dario Kordic, ever?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A witness was testifying yesterday, Colonel Palavra, and one of the members of the Trial Chamber asked the witness whether, regardless of titles, formalities, organograms, things of that sort, whether, in reality, on the ground, de facto, Mr. Kordic was exercising military power and influence over units in Central Bosnia. Now, you were the commander of the military police from August 1st, 1993 until the signature of the Washington Agreement, and well after that. Can you tell us all in this Court: Did Dario Kordic ever try to exert military influence over the soldiers under your -- the military policemen under your command or the soldiers under Colonel Blaskic's command, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as the 4th Police Battalion is concerned, he absolutely never did, as far as the 4th Military Police Battalion is concerned. And I really don't know about other units, but there were the unit commanders, and I don't believe that he would go down to such a level to give orders to units when there are commanders of brigades and the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. Therefore, I do not -- he didn't give me orders, and I don't know that he did to others. I am speaking in my own name and in the name of my unit, so he never commanded me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, initially, when the war -- when the conflict broke out in your country in April of 1992, sir, you took your orders from Ivica Stojak, who was the commander of the HVO municipal staff in Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And during that period of time you never received any instructions, directives, or orders from Mr. Kordic, did you, when you were with the military police administration at the very earliest time, in April, I think, to September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could not have received orders, because the special purpose unit was under the chief of the police administration and Ivo Rezo, who was in command of that unit, through me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then you transferred over to become commander of a special purpose unit in Travnik -- you've told us that -- until the offensive launched by the ABiH in June of 1993, when you came back -- when you came to Vitez. From September of 1992 to June of 1993, sir, did you ever receive any instructions, any directives or orders from Mr. Kordic directed to you as the commander of a special purpose unit, ever?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, never, because Mr. Kordic, he was a much higher level. I may have seen him five times in my whole life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, I would like to ask Colonel Palavra what he means by telling us just now that Mr. Kordic was of a higher level. Colonel, what do you mean by that? Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. As far as I know, in those days Mr. Kordic was engaged in political affairs. He was a politician, and I was in the army; therefore, I had no contact with him whatsoever, nor did I receive any orders. Well, now, the commander of the operative zone of Central Bosnia, Colonel Blaskic, and Mr. Kordic probably did meet and probably they did make certain suggestions. They led the people. Blaskic led them as regards the army and Mr. Kordic as regards civilian things and civilian life. So I could not have any contact. My chief might have. I could through my chief, the chief of the police administration, Ivo Rezo, if I wanted to express an opinion, then I could have done it through him, for him to contact Kordic to deal with certain matters, but I could not have had any meetings with him directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to end up on this, then, sir, as far as you know, speaking with personal experience, initially as the commander of military police, then as a commander of a special purpose unit, and ultimately as commander of the military police again, throughout the wartime period, from April of 1992 until the signature of the Washington agreement in 1994, it's a fact, is it not, and I'll suggest to you that it is a fact, that Mr. Kordic issued no instructions, orders, and in fact had no power or authority over the military police or any of its component special units. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that -- [inaudible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course he can answer the question. Yes, answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I never received a single order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And as far as you know, sir, Mr. Kordic had no authority whatsoever over the military police or any of its component units; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: As far as I know. If somebody knows something else, I don't know anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is, Colonel, that you took your orders from your superior commander who, on August the 1st, was Colonel Blaskic, and he remained your superior commander throughout your time as head of the 4th Battalion of military police, correct; that is, until the signature of the Washington agreement?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then after that, sir, once communications with the headquarters of the military police were reestablished in Ljubuski or Posusje, I think, then you took your orders from the head of the police administration in Posusje who I believe was initially, at least, Valentin Coric?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No. It was Zeljko Siljeg who is now a General.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But even after the signature of the Washington agreement, Mr. Kordic, would it be fair to say, assumed no role whatsoever in the administration of the affairs of the military police or the conduct of the operations of the military police, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, of course not. He had nothing to do with the running of units, any units, including the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you said, sir, that you were appointed on a temporary basis by Colonel Blaskic to your position as commander of the 4th Battalion of military police, but it's true that that temporary appointment by Colonel Blaskic was later confirmed and made permanent by the chief of military police, Valentin Coric; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you have told the Trial Chamber and you told the Blaskic Trial Chamber about the conversations that you had with your commander, Colonel Blaskic, concerning the reorganisation and operations of the military police and the way in which that should be effectuated. Did you ever have any discussions with Mr. Kordic along those lines at any time, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, never, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Throughout the time that you were commander of the 4th Battalion of military police, sir -- and I'll just use 4th Battalion as useful shorthand to include the 7th Battalion when it was known as that as well -- would it be fair to say that you were completely cut off from Kiseljak, and you were not even able to travel to Kiseljak, from August of 1993 until the signature of the Washington agreement in March of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat that question, or rather, the period you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. If you just focus on the time that you were the commander of the 4th Battalion of military police, August of 1993 to March of 1994 when the Washington agreement was signed, you couldn't even travel to Kiseljak, and you never did, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is precisely how it was because after the signing of the agreement between the HVO and the BiH army and the cessation of hostilities, I obtained a special permit signed by the commander in those days of the Muslim units, Alagic, so he gave me special permission to be able to move around the areas under the control of the BiH army. And from our side, two such special permits were issued and signed in those days by Colonel Blaskic, that is, freedom of passage of certain officers who could travel to their units. And I still have that permit here in The Hague in my hotel room. So I had no contact with the military police until the cease-fire was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The permits you've just described, the free passage permits signed by General Alagic, were issued to you after the Washington agreement, I take it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes. We received them after the agreement was signed because in those days, no one dared go to the other side. I remember that I was the first to cross into areas under Muslim control from Kacuni to Bilalovac. Actually, before me, General Filipovic passed and I followed him immediately, because in those days, even with a permit, both sides were afraid to cross into the other side's territory without escort or the military police, either our own police or that of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And what you've just said of Kiseljak, Colonel, is true of Zepce, too: You could not travel to Zepce which was a completely encircled and isolated enclave, from the time that you assumed your command until the signature of the Washington agreement. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes, just so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you yourself didn't even know the commanders, the HVO commanders in those two enclaves, Ivo Lozancic in Zepce and Ivica Rajic in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: No, I didn't know them. It was only after the agreement was signed and after I went to the military police units of the second company in Kiseljak and the third company in Zepce did I meet some of the members of the command, or rather, with my assistant I went to the areas of Kiseljak and Zepce. And then I contacted the commanders announcing my arrival to Rajic and Lozancic that I was coming to familiarise myself in person with the situation in my second and third companies, and that is when I saw them for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And picking up on one of the questions that you were asked this afternoon about Stupni Do, you couldn't get to Vares yourself at any time during the August the 1st, 1993, to March the 31st, 1994, time frame, could you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: I couldn't. Not just I, no one could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And as far as you know, the military police couldn't identify any of the eyewitnesses to the Stupni Do incident on the 23rd of October, 1993, because one week later, the ABiH established full military control over the entire Vares area, and obviously witnesses were unavailable to interview; isn't that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just two final questions before the -- before we break for the day. You were asked some questions about the HIS, the Croatian intelligence service. I only have one question for you on that. That was actually founded in 1995, wasn't it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. And the final question for you today, it's true, is it not, that you actually had people of Muslim ethnicity in the military police amongst the soldiers, the military policemen under your command?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is correct, and I said that in my testimony in Blaskic. In fact, one of the best men in the unit, the best military policeman who had all the commendations and credits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that's a convenient moment, we'll adjourn. Mr. Sayers, was there some matter you wanted to raise, or can it --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There was, Your Honour. I need about five minutes, if we could just let the witness go. Maybe shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel Palavra, that concludes your evidence for today. Would you come back tomorrow morning, please, at half past nine to finish it off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My assistant reminds me that we should get an exhibit number for the package that we distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document will be numbered D344/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The matters that I need to raise today, Your Honour, are these. First, the protective order regarding the Court witness who testified here yesterday restricts access -- it's the same one that was initially entered with respect to Witness AA -- it restricts access just to Mr. Naumovski and myself. Witness AA's protective order was modified to permit disclosure of the testimony to the two -- four people on our team, people that are working on the brief. I wonder if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's extended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. Secondly, I wonder if -- I was a little optimistic when I said we could get our rejoinder papers in on Friday. Given the quantity of material that's being flowing in here and the necessity of evaluating it, I wonder if we could just ask for a one-week extension within which to present our rejoinder exhibit list. I think we can identify witnesses, but we just need a little bit more time to go over the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the third, the third issue concerns the three combat orders that were introduced into evidence yesterday. We may have to go into closed session for that, Your Honour, but you asked us where they came from. I've made inquiries and I now know where they came from, and there is an ancillary issue that needs to be raised with respect to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder if it would be better to deal with that tomorrow when we go into closed session anyway to deal with one or two matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- if you would keep that until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking for a brief explanation. You just granted prolongation of the term for rejoinder. We were not planning to ask for that, but I understand that that benefit would also be for this Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn till half past nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of November, 2000, at 9:30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4:03 p.m., to
